DOC.EP: EC.02.01.01 The hospital manages safety and security risks. EP 1. The hospital identifies safety and security risks associated with the environment of care that could affect patients, staff, and other people coming to the hospital's facilities. Note: Risks are identified from internal sources such as ongoing monitoring of the environment, results of root cause analyses, results of annual proactive risk assessments of high-risk processes, and from credible external sources such as Sentinel Event Alerts. (See also EC.04.01.01, EP 14)
DOC.FINDING: The organization has performed the recommended assessment or proactive risk assessment based on findings and information presented to the organizations EC committee, safety reports, EC rounds data, and incident report data. EC rounds were not analyzed for common issues. However, additional safety concerns were observed and identified during the builidng tour: SPECIFIC FINDINGS: During the walk-through of the facility, the following safety issues were identified: 1. Roof top exhaust ventilation outlets for isolation rooms and laboratory exhaust were not marked or identified as a hazard. 2. In the laboratory, acids and flammables were stored in the same flammable cabinet. 3. In the behavior health unit, the shower emergency alert station is located at chest hieght and not when in reach at floor level.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The organization must label all hazardous exhaust discharge vents located on the roof. TheThe OSHA directive states: Employers must use biological hazard tags on air transport components (e.g., fans, ducts, filters), that may reasonably contain air infected with M. tuberculosis to warn employees, temporary employees, or contractors of possible hazards of contamination [OSHA Directive CPL 02-00-106, (1996)]. ? Example wording for warning label: "Contaminated Air--Respiratory Protection Required." This also applies to the chemo, lab, and other exhaust vents. The organization can make their own or order signs that state similar warnings. ? The laboratory must ensure that only flammable products are stored in the flammable cabinet. Incompatible items, including; Acids, bases, reactive chemicals, and flammables must remain segregated when stored. ? All shower emergency alert devices must be lowered to within 4-6 inches of floor level.

DOC.EP: EC.02.02.01 The hospital manages risks related to hazardous materials and waste. EP 5. The hospital minimizes risks associated with selecting, handling, storing, transporting, using, and disposing of hazardous chemicals.
DOC.FINDING: In the laboratory, the eyewash stations are missing covers. Two eyewash handheld devices are missing the reqiured plastic cover that protects the opening from being contaminated.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The plastic covers must be replaced for these identified eyewashes.

DOC.EP: EC.02.03.03 The hospital conducts fire drills. EP 2. The hospital conducts fire drills every 12 months from the date of the last drill in all freestanding buildings classified as business occupancies and in which patients are seen or treated. Note: In leased or rented facilities, drills need be conducted only in areas of the building that the hospital occupies.
DOC.FINDING: For the Blackwell CBOC, the organization has not performed the required annual fire drill. A fire drill with response critique was not completed annually.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The organization must ensure that all CBOC locations have completed an annual fire drill. ? The drill must be critqued and improvements (if required) must be listed.

DOC.EP: EC.02.03.05 The hospital maintains fire safety equipment and fire safety building features. Note: This standard does not require hospitals to have the types of fire safety equipment and building features described below. However, if these types of equipment or features exist within the building, then the following maintenance, testing, and inspection requirements apply. EP 1. At least quarterly, the hospital tests supervisory signal devices (except valve tamper switches). The completion date of the tests is documented. Note: For additional guidance on performing tests, see NFPA 72, 1999 edition (Table 7-3.2).
DOC.FINDING: The hospital failed to document at least quarterly the activation of the following supervisory signal devices for the fire pumps: Electric Fire Pump: 1. Fire pump loss of power 2. Phase reversal 3. Not in auto
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The organization must document the activation and completion of these tests at least quaterly. EP 2. Every 6 months, the hospital tests valve tamper switches and water-flow devices. The completion date of the tests is documented. Note: For additional guidance on performing tests, see NFPA 72, 1999 edition (Table 7-3.2).
DOC.FINDING: Review of records for this element revealed that the testing was performed only one time and not semiannually as required by the VA.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The organization must ensure that all flow and tamper switches are tested at least semi annually. EP 6. For automatic sprinkler systems: Every week, the hospital tests fire pumps under no-flow conditions. The completion date of the tests is documented. Note: For additional guidance on performing tests, see NFPA 25, 1998 edition.
DOC.FINDING: Review of test records for this element revealed that not all required items were effectively addressed or listed.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: The organization must ensure that all testing records indicate the following items: 1. Name of test/activity, including number of devices tested, number passed, number failed. 2. Date completed. 3. Required frequency. 4. Name and contact information of person conducting the test. 5. NFPA standard. 6. Results or test. 7. Recommendations and follow-up if applicable. EP 10. For automatic sprinkler systems: Every quarter, the hospital inspects all fire department water supply connections. The completion dates of the inspections are documented. Note: For additional guidance on performing tests, see NFPA 25, 1998 edition (Section 9-7.1).
DOC.FINDING: Review of test records for this element revealed that not all required items were effectively addressed or listed. Code reference was missing from the record.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: The organization must ensure that all testing records indicate the following items: 1. Name of test/activity, including number of devices tested, number passed, number failed. 2. Date completed. 3. Required frequency. 4. Name and contact information of person conducting the test. 5. NFPA standard. 6. Results or test. 7. Recommendations and follow-up if applicable. EP 11. For automatic sprinkler systems: Every 12 months, the hospital tests fire pumps under flow. The completion date of the tests is documented. Note: For additional guidance on performing tests, see NFPA 25, 1998 edition.
DOC.FINDING: The annual fire pump testing was conducted. However, the test results graphed for the electrical fire pump indicated the performance was less than desired. The test results indicate that net flow is less than 95% of performace requirements. The report states as a recommendation "pump needs repacking". There was no action taken on the results listed or test engineers recommendation.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? Testing data for fire pumps must be acted on when results are communicated to the hospital. The pump performance curve and collected data must be compared. Variances more that 5% of the manufacturers performance data require follow-up and investigation. ? The organization must evaluate the pump and make recommended repairs listed in the test report. EP 13. Every 6 months, the hospital inspects any automatic fire- extinguishing systems in a kitchen. The completion dates of the inspections are documented. Note 1: Discharge of the fire-extinguishing systems is not required. Note 2: For additional guidance on performing inspections, see NFPA 96, 1998 edition.
DOC.FINDING: Review of records for this element revealed that the testing was performed only one time and not semiannually as required. Records were missing for August 2012.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: The organization must ensure that all testing is completed semiannually. EP 18. The hospital operates fire and smoke dampers 1 year after installation and then at least every 6 years to verify that they fully close. The completion date of the tests is documented. Note 1: The initial test that must occur 1 year after installation applies only to dampers installed on and after January 1, 2008. Note 2: For additional guidance, see NFPA 80 Standard for Fire Doors and Other Opening Protectives, 2007 edition (Section 19.4.1.1) and NFPA 105, 2007 edition (Section 6.5.2).

DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The organization must complete the required testing for this element. Test records must indicate the following items: ? 1. Name of test/activity, including number of fire damper and smoke damper devices tested, number passed, number failed. ? 2. Date completed. ? 3. Required frequency. ? 4. Name and contact information of person conducting the test. ? 5. NFPA standard. ? 6. Results or test. ? 7. Recommendations and follow-up if applicable. EP 19. Every 12 months, the hospital tests automatic smoke-detection shutdown devices for air-handling equipment. The completion date of the tests is documented. Note: For additional guidance on performing tests, see NFPA 90A, Standard for the Installation of Air Conditioning and Ventilation Systems, 1999 edition (Section 4-4.1). 0

DOC.EP: EC.02.04.03 The hospital inspects, tests, and maintains medical equipment. EP 2. The hospital inspects, tests, and maintains all life-support equipment. These activities are documented. (See also EC.02.04.01, EPs 3 and 4; PC.02.01.11, EP 2)
DOC.FINDING: During discussion of AED testing, it was revealed that the organization preforms a two year check on the equipment as required by the manufacturer. However, the equipment (AED) is life support and requires more frequent testing and examination. The organization is not preforming the additional inspections.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The organization must develop a method to maintain AED's as life support equipment. ? The following is listed on The Joint Commission site under FAQ: Life Support Equipment: Any device used for the purpose of sustaining life and whose failure to perform its primary function, when used according to manufacturer’s instructions and clinical protocol, will lead to patient death in the absence of immediate intervention (examples include ventilators, heart-lung bypass machines). Defibrillation is a response to life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias, ventricular fibrillation and ventricular tachycardia. Defibrillation consists of delivering a therapeutic dose of electricity to the affected heart with a defibrillator. The dose of electricity restores a normal heart rhythm, allowing the heart to continue to function in the patient. Therefore, the Joint Commission considers defibrillators life support equipment. As it is required that organizations maintain an inventory of all medical equipment or selected medical equipment categorized by physical risk associated with use (including all life support equipment), defibrillators must be included in an organization's medical equipment inventory. Maintenance activities then must be identified for equipment on the inventory. A maintenance strategy for defibrillators could include a range of activities from a visual inspection of the single-use AED (automatic external defibrillator) to the daily testing of a defibrillator in clinical use settings based on organization policy.

DOC.EP: EC.02.05.05 The hospital inspects, tests, and maintains utility systems. Note: At times, maintenance is performed by an external service. In these cases, hospitals are not required to possess maintenance documentation but must have access to such documentation during survey and as needed. EP 1. The hospital tests utility system components on the inventory before initial use. The completion date of the tests is documented. (See also EC.02.05.01, EP 2)
DOC.FINDING: During review of PM (preventiative maintenace) test records for utility system, it was revealed that ICE machines and other items must be tested at an assigned interval. The PM requirements indicate that Ice machines will be inspected monthly and semi-annually. The test documentation did not indicate that these insepections have been done since June 2012. NOTE: The organization was cited on this item last TJC survey.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The organization must review all PM intervals and documentation defined for critical utitlies. Based on the hospitals defined PM intervals, the test documentation must indicate the item was complete. This issus appears to exist for multiple utitlies, including (AHU) Air Handler Unit filter changes. The tests and inspections may have been completed however, the documentation did not reflect that it was done. ? The organization must review all PM records for utilties and ensure that inspections are completed and documented as completed.

DOC.EP: EC.02.05.07 The hospital inspects, tests, and maintains emergency power systems. Note: This standard does not require hospitals to have the types of emergency power equipment discussed below. However, if these types of equipment exist within the building, then the following maintenance, testing, and inspection requirements apply. EP 1. At 30-day intervals, the hospital performs a functional test of battery-powered lights required for egress for a minimum duration of 30 seconds. The completion date of the tests is documented.
DOC.FINDING: 1. Battery operated lighting test were conducted in the hospital monthly. The test documentation did not indicate the time frame for the test. 2. Documentation that battery operated exit signs and emergency power lights for egress was not provided for CBOC.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The organization must document all battery operated testing monthly. The organization must modify its documentation to indicate test procedure. ? The battery operated testing must be compelted for all devices in the CBOC locations. A list of devices must be constructed and test documents must indicate monthly testing is completed. ? The test documentation must indicate the following: 1. Date the test was completed. 2. 30 second testing. 3. Results of test and any actions completed. EP 2. Every 12 months, the hospital either performs a functional test of battery-powered lights required for egress for a duration of 1 1/2 hours; or the hospital replaces all batteries every 12 months and, during replacement, performs a random test of 10% of all batteries for 1 1/2 hours. The completion date of the tests is documented.
DOC.FINDING: During evaluation of documentation, there was no record that annual testing was completed at the hospital or CBOC locations.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The organization must indicate that annual battery operated testing is completed at the hospital and CBOC locations. ? The test documentation must indicate the following: 1. Date the test was completed. 2. 90 minute testing. 3. Results of test and any action completed. EP 6. Twelve times a year, at intervals of not less than 20 days and not more than 40 days, the hospital tests all automatic transfer switches. The completion date of the tests is documented.
DOC.FINDING: The hospital is testing the generator monthly by activating a ATS. That ATS is listed as activated. The remainder of the ATS assocaited with the gererator set are activated, but not documented as tested. Test documentation did not indicate that each ATS was activated.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The organization must list all ATS and indicate they are activated at least monthly. EP 7. At least once every 36 months, hospitals with a generator providing emergency power for the services listed in EC.02.05.03, EPs 5 and 6, test each emergency generator for a minimum of 4 continuous hours. The completion date of the tests is documented. Note: For additional guidance, see NFPA 110, 2005 edition, Standard for Emergency and Standby Power Systems.
DOC.FINDING: During the evaluation, the organization did not provide documentation that this items was completed.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The organization must maintain documentation indicating that each generator is tested every 36 months for 4 continuous hours at 30% load or greater. The documentation must be recorded and logged, with loads, at least every 30 minutes on the test sheet.

DOC.EP: EC.02.05.09 The hospital inspects, tests, and maintains medical gas and vacuum systems. Note: This standard does not require hospitals to have the medical gas and vacuum systems discussed below. However, if a hospital has these types of systems, then the following inspection, testing, and maintenance requirements apply. EP 1. In time frames defined by the hospital, the hospital inspects, tests, and maintains critical components of piped medical gas systems, including master signal panels, area alarms, automatic pressure switches, shutoff valves, flexible connectors, and outlets. These activities are documented. (See also EC.02.05.01, EP 3)
DOC.FINDING: 1. The medical gas system policy states that the master gas panel alarms will be checked monthly (as required by NFPA 99). Documentation indicates that this has not occurred since December 2012. 2. The policy states that annual testing of the medical gas system components will be completed. The documentation of testing did not indicate the zone shut-off and patient room gas connections were tested routinely. 3. The organizations written policy did describe the components for testing, testing frequency, reference to manufacturer, and industry approved standards for inspection and testing of the medical gas and vacuum systems. The policy states that nitrogen and nitrous oxide manifolds and systems will be checked monthly. There was no indication that the test or checks were completed. NOTE: The organization was cited for this last TJC survey.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The organization must review it medical gas system test policy and ensure that all inspection are completed and documented. EP 3. The hospital makes main supply valves and area shutoff valves for piped medical gas and vacuum systems accessible and clearly identifies what the valves control.
DOC.FINDING: Medical gas shut-off systems were blocked in the folloiwng areas: 1. On several nursing units, the gas shut off was blocked by a door. 2. Surgery department, vlocked by equipment in hall.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? Medical gas shut off valves must be visible and unobstructed. The organization must remove items from in front of valves and ensure access on each unit.

DOC.EP: EC.02.06.05 The hospital manages its environment during demolition, renovation, or new construction to reduce risk to those in the organization. EP 2. When planning for demolition, construction, or renovation, the hospital conducts a preconstruction risk assessment for air quality requirements, infection control, utility requirements, noise, vibration, and other hazards that affect care, treatment, and services. Note: See LS.01.02.01 for information on fire safety procedures to implement during construction or renovation.
DOC.FINDING: See EP 3.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? See EP 3. EP 3. The hospital takes action based on its assessment to minimize risks during demolition, construction, or renovation.
DOC.FINDING: 1. Review of the 5th floor construction and renovation project in the hostpial revealed the folloiwng: (Class III/IV precautions identified on ICRA form): a. No moniotoring of negative air. b. Barriers did not contain the space (above the ceiling) and were not appropriate. 2. The ICRA did not indicate that noise, vibration, or pressurization was evaluted.
DOC.RECOMMENDED: ? The hospital must implement proper precaustions during times of construction and dust generation activities. These precautions include: a. Isolation of HVAC systems components from possible construciton debries. b. Use of appropriate negative pressurization devices. c. Monitoring of pressurization and maintaining presure at least negative 0.03 inches H2O. d. Provide appropriate barrrier protection. The ICRA protocols did not dictate what the hospitals policy is for discontinuation of precausions. The need to evaluated of approve certain conditions prior to removal of negative air and barrieres was not outlined.
